name: Bianca Santos

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time. I'm from the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions or government. Everything you tell me is confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I work at Shopfloor, a company that runs online shops for small retailers, like bakeries and bike shops. I'm a junior developer on the checkout team, so I deal with the bit where people pay. Most of my day is fixing things like a discount code that doesn't apply, or a card payment that fails on one bank. I started as a tester two years ago and moved over to coding last spring.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like about the work, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I like that checkout is where it matters. If my code breaks, a little bakery loses a sale, and I take that seriously. What wears me out is being on call one week a month, because payments break at 2 a.m. I use the AI chat sometimes, when the others swear by something and I've seen it work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it was useful, overhyped, and now we can get on with things. At work I'd probably be the one saying I told you it would settle down. Online I'd keep quiet, I'm not a big poster.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For me it means steady work. Checkout code is fiddly and full of edge cases, the odd situations nobody planned for, and that's still people's work in a plateau. I'd keep slowly improving.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep going on the checkout team and push to come off the on-call rota by next summer. I'd use the AI chat a bit more for tests, now that everyone agrees what it's good for. And I'd keep putting money aside, because of the restaurant.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly settled, with one worry I'd already have anyway, which is my partner's job.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything at home that's on your mind, even in this calm version?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes, the restaurant. My partner Diego is a chef, and his restaurant has cut his shifts twice this year. If it closes, my pay carries us, and we've got about eight months saved, so it's fine, but it's on my mind.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to the bakery owners you work for?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell them nothing's changing on our side. Your checkout still works, your fees stay the same. Most of them just want to sell bread.

I'd be the one saying it would **settle down**.

Use the AI chat a bit more for **tests**.
Keep **saving** in case Diego's restaurant closes.
feel: Mostly **settled**, with an existing worry about her **partner's job**.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's real and we should be practical about it. Learn the tools, keep your skills, don't panic. I'd say that at work, and I'd mean it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, it's not great for me. I'm junior, and coding and checking are exactly what's on the list. If Shopfloor (her employer) needs fewer of us, I'd want to be the one who knows the payment rules best, not the one who types fastest.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd start using the AI tools every day within a month, once a couple of the seniors show me how. I'd apply to the in-house payments team at a big bank within a year, because banks move slowly. And I'd hold off on the wedding savings and keep them as an emergency fund.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. Not shaking, but I'd check job boards on my phone at night.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who on the checkout team would go first?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably the testers first, my old job, then juniors like me. Our senior, Hannah, would be fine, because someone has to say yes or no to what the AI writes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If you moved to a bank, would that really be safer?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Safer for a few years, I think. Banks are careful with payments because the rules are strict. That buys time, and time is what I'd want.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the government needs to move fast, and I'd say it to anyone. I'm normally in the middle on things, but this is too big to leave to companies.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think my job is gone within a year or so. Checkout code is pure thinking work. A junior who moved over from testing isn't who a company keeps.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd sit down with Diego and plan a food stall, his cooking and my business side, because cooking is hands-on. I'd cut every spending line except rent and food. And I'd keep coding at Shopfloor as long as they paid me, saving everything.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. The speed is the frightening part. Two years isn't enough to do anything properly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Thinking AI first, robots three years later. What does that mean for you and Diego?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It flips us. For years my job was the safe one and my partner's was shaky. With robots three years behind, a chef's cooking would outlast my coding. I'd be the one learning Diego's trade.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do with the wedding?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We'd postpone it. A wedding is a lot of money, and I'd rather put that into the stall. Our families would complain, but they'd understand.

I'd say this is **too big** to leave to companies.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we've got a few years to get this right, so let's not waste them. Train people, plan for it. That's the practical line.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I'd get maybe three more years in software. That's enough to save hard and get some business experience. Then I'd want something with my hands in it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd stay at Shopfloor and save a third of my pay. I'd take an evening course in small business accounts in year one. And in year three, I'd put about half our savings into a food truck with Diego.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but with a plan. It feels more like a project than a cliff.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would the food stall still be the plan with five years?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes, but done properly. Two years in, test it at weekend markets first. If it doesn't make money on Saturdays, it won't make money full-time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What's the risk you're not seeing?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That everyone has the same idea. If every office worker opens a food truck, the market is going to be crowded. I'd have to be better, or different.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is enough to plan, so plan. I'd tell younger people at work to build skills that last and keep some savings. Very sensible, very me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd have a real software career first, maybe reach mid-level, maybe even senior. But I'd still be leaving it in my late thirties. That's the bit that bothers me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep going at Shopfloor and aim for mid-level in two years. I'd keep saving a fifth of my pay into an index fund. And I'd let the food truck idea wait until about 2031.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, quietly. It's ten years away but it's still the end of what I trained for.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Ten years. Do you still need the food truck?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably, in the end. I'd want the food truck as a second act, not a lifeboat. Diego would be happy, it's his dream anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would this change when you'd get married?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No, we'd get married next year as planned. Ten years is long enough that a wedding isn't the thing to cut.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028. We'd be starting a business in a panic, with half the city doing the same. What would help is cheap start-up loans for small hands-on businesses, and some help with rent while people switch.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe ask about couples. In my house, the question isn't just my job, it's which of our two jobs lasts longer.
